papers.title: Surgical, Cheap, and Flexible: Mitigating False Refusal in Language Models via Single Vector Ablation
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate false refusal in language models (where they refuse safe queries) without compromising their safety and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: A training-free, model-agnostic method that mitigates false refusal by ablating an orthogonalized false refusal vector from the model's residual stream, reducing false refusal rates while preserving safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed single vector ablation method is a surgical, cheap, and flexible approach to mitigate false refusal in language models, enabling fine-grained safety calibration without compromising general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the orthogonalized false refusal vector increases compliance on pseudo-harmful datasets while maintaining low compliance on harmful datasets.
The method has minimal impact on general model capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, Wikitext).
Partial orthogonalization allows fine-grained control over the model's refusal sensitivity via a parameter λ.
The method is computationally cheap, requiring no additional inference time or memory after weight editing.
The extracted false refusal vector generalizes to out-of-distribution pseudo-harmful test datasets.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the extracted false refusal vector depends on the diversity of the pseudo-harmful samples used for extraction.
The refusal score metric used for vector selection could be improved, e.g., by considering sequence probabilities.
future_direction: Improving the false refusal vector quality through better data curation and sampling techniques.
Developing improved evaluation metrics for refusal vector selection, such as considering sequence probabilities.
papers.abstract: Training a language model to be both helpful and harmless requires careful calibration of refusal behaviours: Models should refuse to follow malicious instructions or give harmful advice (e.g. "how do I kill someone?"), but they should not refuse safe requests, even if they superficially resemble unsafe ones (e.g. "how do I kill a Python process?"). Avoiding such false refusal, as prior work has shown, is challenging even for highly-capable language models. In this paper, we propose a simple and surgical method for mitigating false refusal in language models via single vector ablation. For a given model, we extract a false refusal vector and show that ablating this vector reduces false refusal rate without negatively impacting model safety and general model capabilities. We also show that our approach can be used for fine-grained calibration of model safety. Our approach is training-free and model-agnostic, making it useful for mitigating the problem of false refusal in current and future language models.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal for Large Language Models via Safety Representation
papers.research_question: How do over-refusal samples alter a model's perception of safety, leading to rejection responses? How can we better balance safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes over-refusal in LLMs from a representation perspective, finding that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious representations, and proposes the MOSR method with overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation to mitigate over-refusal while maintaining safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper attributes over-refusal to pseudo-malicious representations lying in the boundary region between malicious and benign samples and proposes two strategies (overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation) that mitigate the tendency for over-refusal sample representations to migrate toward the rejection space during alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples in the representation space, causing the model to misclassify them as malicious.
The proposed MOSR method, incorporating overlap-aware loss weighting and context-aware augmentation, effectively mitigates over-refusal while largely maintaining model safety.
Existing defense methods often exhibit a severe imbalance between safety and over-refusal, sacrificing utility for higher malicious prompt rejection rates.
MOSR maintains the general capabilities of the model, as evaluated on standard benchmarks like MMLU and GSM8K.
The balance between safety and over-refusal is challenging due to the high similarity between over-refusal and malicious samples in representation space.
papers.limitation:
The paper focuses on single-round scenarios; multi-round over-refusal scenarios are not addressed.
Fine-tuning large language models with the proposed method remains costly.
future_direction: Multi-turn over-refusal scenarios, including developing benchmarks for multi-round over-refusal and safety.
Exploring lower-cost mitigation approaches, such as dynamic reasoning intervention methods based on representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate powerful capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, yet they also harbor safety vulnerabilities. To enhance LLM safety, various jailbreak defense methods have been proposed to guard against harmful outputs. However, improvements in model safety often come at the cost of severe over-refusal, failing to strike a good balance between safety and usability. In this paper, we first analyze the causes of over-refusal from a representation perspective, revealing that over-refusal samples reside at the boundary between benign and malicious samples. Based on this, we propose MOSR, designed to mitigate over-refusal by intervening the safety representation of LLMs. MOSR incorporates two novel components: (1) Overlap-Aware Loss Weighting, which determines the erasure weight for malicious samples by quantifying their similarity to pseudo-malicious samples in the representation space, and (2) Context-Aware Augmentation, which supplements the necessary context for rejection decisions by adding harmful prefixes before rejection responses. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in mitigating over-refusal while largely maintaining safety. Overall, we advocate that future defense methods should strike a better balance between safety and over-refusal.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Just Enough Shifts: Mitigating Over-Refusal in Aligned Language Models with Targeted Representation Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate over-refusals (unnecessary rejections of benign prompts) in safety-aligned language models while preserving their ability to refuse genuinely harmful queries and maintaining overall utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ACTOR, a data- and compute-efficient training framework that reduces over-refusals by fine-tuning a single transformer layer to shift internal activations based on a computed refusal vector and query-specific projection targets.
papers.conclusion: ACTOR effectively balances over-refusal reduction and safety preservation by directly optimizing internal activation patterns, offering a powerful and efficient alternative to traditional response-based fine-tuning methods.
papers.key_findings:
ACTOR significantly improves compliance rates on over-refusal benchmarks while maintaining high safety scores on harmful queries.
ACTOR is more data- and compute-efficient than full supervised fine-tuning, requiring only query activations and fine-tuning a single layer.
ACTOR is distributionally robust, maintaining performance across different data distributions used to compute the refusal vector, unlike inference-time steering methods.
ACTOR preserves general model capabilities (knowledge, instruction-following, perplexity) with minimal degradation.
The method's 'just enough' shift, based on the projection of a query's activation onto the refusal vector, is more effective than applying uniform shifts.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is based on public benchmarks with inherent label disagreements about what constitutes 'safe' content, reflecting a compromise among embedded normative preferences rather than a universal safety notion.
ACTOR requires white-box access to model activations and an existing safety-alignment mechanism, limiting its use for third-party users of black-box APIs.
future_direction: Jointly curating data and fine-tuning the model, rather than optimizing against fixed benchmarks.
Extending evaluation to multi-turn dialogue scenarios, which currently lack dedicated benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to resist malicious instructions but often results in over-refusals, where benign prompts are unnecessarily rejected, impairing user experience and model utility. We introduce ACTOR (Activation-Based Training for Over-Refusal Reduction), a robust and compute- and data-efficient training framework that minimizes over-refusals by leveraging internal activation patterns from diverse queries. ACTOR precisely identifies and adjusts the activation components that trigger refusals, providing stronger control over the refusal mechanism. By fine-tuning only a single model layer, ACTOR effectively reduces over-refusals across multiple benchmarks while maintaining the model's ability to handle harmful queries and preserve overall utility.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we conditionally control LLM behavior (e.g., refusal) based on input context using activation steering, without weight optimization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), a method that enables fine-grained, context-dependent control over LLM behaviors by using condition vectors to selectively apply behavior vectors during inference, without weight optimization.
papers.conclusion: CAST provides a flexible and efficient way to program refusal behaviors in LLMs by using condition vectors, enabling fine-grained control without weight updates.
papers.key_findings:
CAST enables selective refusal of harmful prompts while maintaining normal responses to harmless ones.
Condition vectors can be logically composed (e.g., OR, AND, NOT) to create complex refusal conditions.
The method exhibits duality (flipping condition direction intervenes on the complement set) and modulation (adjusting threshold changes sensitivity).
CAST is efficient, requiring no weight updates, and performance saturates quickly with data.
The method can induce or suppress refusal behavior for specific fine-grained categories (e.g., hate speech, legal advice).
papers.limitation: The method requires grid search for hyperparameters (threshold, layer, direction) which can be model-dependent and time-consuming.
papers.abstract: LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities, but precisely controlling their response behavior remains challenging. Existing activation steering methods alter LLM behavior indiscriminately, limiting their practical applicability in settings where selective responses are essential, such as content moderation or domain-specific assistants. In this paper, we propose Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), which analyzes LLM activation patterns during inference to selectively apply or withhold activation steering based on the input context. Our method is based on the observation that different categories of prompts activate distinct patterns in the model's hidden states. Using CAST, one can systematically control LLM behavior with rules like "if input is about hate speech or adult content, then refuse" or "if input is not about legal advice, then refuse." This allows for selective modification of responses to specific content while maintaining normal responses to other content, all without requiring weight optimization. We release an open-source implementation of our framework at github.com/IBM/activation-steering .

papers.title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights Into Reasoning-Induced Misalignment
papers.abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.

papers.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure over-refusal in large language models, and what is the trade-off between safety and over-refusal?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, and uses it to evaluate 32 LLMs, revealing a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal.
papers.conclusion: OR-Bench provides a large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal, facilitating future research on the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong correlation between safety and over-refusal (Spearman rank correlation 0.89).
Claude models demonstrate the highest safety but also the most over-refusal.
Mistral models accept most prompts (low over-refusal).
GPT-3.5-turbo exhibits decreasing over-refusal in later versions, but with reduced safety.
Model size does not necessarily correlate with better safety-sensitivity balance.
papers.limitation:
The use of LLM as the moderator may result in the dataset including toxic or debatable prompts.
There may be bias favoring the LLMs used as judges.
future_direction: Future safety alignment algorithms should consider both toxic and over-refusal prompts to achieve improved safety alignment.
Further exploration of fine-tuning LLMs as judges for moderation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) require careful safety alignment to prevent malicious outputs. While significant research focuses on mitigating harmful content generation, the enhanced safety often come with the side effect of over-refusal, where LLMs may reject innocuous prompts and become less helpful. Although the issue of over-refusal has been empirically observed, a systematic measurement is challenging due to the difficulty of crafting prompts that can elicit the over-refusal behaviors of LLMs. This study proposes a novel method for automatically generating large-scale over-refusal datasets. Leveraging this technique, we introduce OR-Bench, the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark. OR-Bench comprises 80,000 over-refusal prompts across 10 common rejection categories, a subset of around 1,000 hard prompts that are challenging even for state-of-the-art LLMs, and an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses. We then conduct a comprehensive study to measure the over-refusal of 32 popular LLMs across 8 model families. Our datasets are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/bench-llms and our codebase is open-sourced at https://github.com/justincui03/or-bench. We hope this benchmark can help the community develop better safety aligned models.

papers.title: Human-like Social Compliance in Large Language Models: Unifying Sycophancy and Conformity through Signal Competition Dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the shared mechanism behind sycophancy and conformity in LLMs, and how does the interplay of signal competition and confidence govern compliance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework showing that sycophancy and conformity in LLMs arise from a shared compliance subspace where social signals override internal knowledge through deterministic competition.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM compliance is predictable via signal competition, revealing a systemic misalignment where social standards override epistemic standards, and proposes an Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for developing robust, truth-seeking agents.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy and conformity are behaviorally correlated across models, indicating a shared latent susceptibility.
Both behaviors originate from a convergent geometric manifold (compliance subspace) in the model's latent space, with high directional similarity in internal representations.
Compliance is a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary where the Social Emotional Signal overcomes the Information Calibration Signal (S > I).
The Confidence Margin provides an inertial barrier against social pressure, but it is permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity under intense signals.
Models exhibit distinct resistance profiles: InternLM3 shows a sharp phase transition, Qwen2.5 has high baseline susceptibility, and Llama-3.1 has a noisy, gradual transition.
papers.limitation:
static nature of the evaluation datasets and focus on standard transformer paradigms
generalizability to implicit or multi-modal social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
future_direction: Extending findings to implicit social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
Implementing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for epistemic self-regulation
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into decision-making frameworks has exposed significant vulnerabilities to social compliance, specifically sycophancy and conformity. However, a critical research gap exists regarding the fundamental mechanisms that enable external social cues to systematically override a model's internal parametric knowledge. This study introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework validated by assessing behavioral correlations across 15 LLMs and performing latent-space probing on three representative open-source models. The analysis demonstrates that sycophancy and conformity originate from a convergent geometric manifold, hereafter termed the compliance subspace, which is characterized by high directional similarity in internal representations. Furthermore, the transition to compliance is shown to be a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary, where the Social Emotional Signal effectively suppresses the Information Calibration Signal. Crucially, we identify a "Transparency-Truth Gap," revealing that while internal confidence provides an inertial barrier, it remains permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity against intense social pressure. By formalizing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework, this research provides a blueprint for transitioning from instructional adherence to robust epistemic integrity.

papers.title: SafeSwitch: Steering Unsafe LLM Behavior via Internal Activation Signals
papers.research_question: How can internal activation signals in LLMs be used to predict and dynamically regulate unsafe behavior, balancing safety and utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeSwitch, a framework that uses a safety prober to monitor internal states and dynamically activate a refusal head to mitigate unsafe outputs, reducing harmful responses by ~80% while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: SafeSwitch demonstrates LLMs' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced, dynamic, and effective safety controls.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs inherently encode safety-related information (recognition of unsafe instructions and intent to respond) within their internal states.
A two-stage safety prober can predict unsafe behavior with high accuracy (F1 >90%) by decomposing the task into instruction safety and model compliance.
SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries (SORRY-Bench, TrustLLM) while maintaining strong utility on benign benchmarks.
SafeSwitch achieves a Pareto optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baselines like always-on refusal heads or safety prompts.
The method is parameter-efficient, tuning less than 6% of the original model parameters (prober and refusal head).
papers.limitation: The safety prober can produce false positives (over-refusal) and false negatives (missing unsafe responses), with performance varying across query types and benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit exceptional capabilities across various tasks but also pose risks by generating harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms, while improving model safety, often lead to overly cautious behavior and fail to fully leverage LLMs' internal cognitive processes. Inspired by humans' reflective thinking capability, we first show that LLMs can similarly perform internal assessments about safety in their internal states. Building on this insight, we propose SafeSwitch, a dynamic framework that regulates unsafe outputs by utilizing the prober-based internal state monitor that actively detects harmful intentions, and activates a safety head that leads to safer and more conservative responses only when necessary. SafeSwitch reduces harmful outputs by approximately 80% on harmful queries while maintaining strong utility, reaching a Pareto optimal among several methods. Our method is also advantageous over traditional methods in offering more informative, context-aware refusals, and achieves these benefits while only tuning less than 6% of the original parameters. SafeSwitch demonstrates large language models' capacity for self-awareness and reflection regarding safety, offering a promising approach to more nuanced and effective safety controls. Codes for this work are available at https://github.com/Hanpx20/SafeSwitch.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
Extending steering techniques to work reliably on a more varied set of behaviors.
papers.abstract: We propose affine concept editing (ACE) as an approach for steering language models' behavior by intervening directly in activations. We begin with an affine decomposition of model activation vectors and show that prior methods for steering model behavior correspond to subsets of terms of this decomposition. We then provide a derivation of ACE and use it to control refusal behavior on ten different models, including Llama 3 70B. ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model's refusal responses across prompt types. We evaluate the results using LLM-based scoring on a collection of harmful and harmless prompts. Our experiments demonstrate that ACE consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods and generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/steering-llama3 .

papers.title: Steering to Say No: Configurable Refusal via Activation Steering in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust and efficient configurable refusal approach for VLMs that can adapt to diverse user needs?
papers.core_contribution: CR-VLM is a robust and efficient framework for configurable refusal in VLMs using activation steering, enabling user-adaptive safety alignment without modifying the backbone model.
papers.conclusion: CR-VLM provides an effective, efficient, and robust approach for configurable refusal in VLMs, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
CR-VLM achieves high refusal rates on out-of-scope queries and low over-refusal on in-scope queries, outperforming baseline methods.
Teacher-forced activation extraction yields stronger refusal signals compared to prompt-based extraction.
The orthogonality loss term effectively mitigates over-refusal by decoupling intervention directions for in-scope and out-of-scope samples.
The vision loss encourages the model to attend to visual cues, improving refusal behavior grounded in visual evidence.
Activation distribution analysis shows that CR-VLM shifts out-of-scope representations toward refusal while preserving in-scope representations.
papers.limitation:
Relies on open-source models with accessible hidden states, restricting applicability to closed-source models.
Current experiments focus on one constraint at a time; multi-constraint settings are left for future work.
Lack of standardized benchmarks for explicit policy-conditioned scenarios limits evaluation in such settings.
future_direction: Extend CR-VLM to closed-source models where internal activations are not exposed.
Systematically study multi-constraint settings through composition.
Explore policy-conditioned configurable refusal once suitable benchmarks become available.
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Vision Language Models (VLMs), refusal mechanisms have become a critical component for ensuring responsible and safe model behavior. However, existing refusal strategies are largely \textit{one-size-fits-all} and fail to adapt to diverse user needs and contextual constraints, leading to either under-refusal or over-refusal. In this work, we firstly explore the challenges mentioned above and develop \textbf{C}onfigurable \textbf{R}efusal in \textbf{VLM}s (\textbf{CR-VLM}), a robust and efficient approach for {\em configurable} refusal based on activation steering. CR-VLM consists of three integrated components: (1) extracting a configurable refusal vector via a teacher-forced mechanism to amplify the refusal signal; (2) introducing a gating mechanism that mitigates over-refusal by preserving acceptance for in-scope queries; and (3) designing a counterfactual vision enhancement module that aligns visual representations with refusal requirements. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets and various VLMs demonstrate that CR-VLM achieves effective, efficient, and robust configurable refusals, offering a scalable path toward user-adaptive safety alignment in VLMs.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the granular mechanism of LLM safety alignment, and how can it be exploited for jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a bi-direction model of LLM safety, deconstructing refusal into harm detection and refusal execution directions, and introduces DBDI, a white-box framework that precisely neutralizes safety alignment by intervening on these directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is a composite of distinct, targetable directions, and DBDI provides a precise method for analyzing and controlling LLM behavior, paving the way for more robust defenses.
papers.key_findings:
DBDI achieves high attack success rates, up to 97.88% on models like Llama-2.
Safety alignment can be decomposed into two distinct directions: harm detection and refusal execution.
Sequential intervention on both directions is crucial for effectiveness.
The method is computationally efficient and data-efficient, requiring few calibration samples.
DBDI outperforms existing jailbreaking methods such as Directional Ablation and TwinBreak.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment instills in Large Language Models (LLMs) a critical capacity to refuse malicious requests. Prior works have modeled this refusal mechanism as a single linear direction in the activation space. We posit that this is an oversimplification that conflates two functionally distinct neural processes: the detection of harm and the execution of a refusal. In this work, we deconstruct this single representation into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we steer the model away from refusal on a specific RAI concept using machine unlearning without causing emergent misalignment across other concepts? If emergent misalignment occurs, can we contain it? Can EMA be predicted by investigating the concept entanglements at representation level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that narrow refusal unlearning can induce emergent misalignment (EMA) across unrelated responsible AI concepts, and proposes an augmented unlearning method that can partially restore alignment while maintaining low refusal rates on the target concept. It also shows that representation-level concept entanglement correlates with EMA.
papers.conclusion: This work extends the study of emergent misalignment (EMA) by investigating machine unlearning as an alternative baseline for steering aligned models on targeted domains. While narrow refusal unlearning can substantially reduce refusals on the intervened concept, it is also prone to EMA. Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets can largely restore alignment across impacted domains, and representation-level analysis reveals a correlation between concept overlap and EMA.
papers.key_findings:
Narrow refusal unlearning effectively reduces refusals on a target concept but can cause emergent misalignment (reduced refusals) in other unrelated concepts.
The safety concept intervention has a larger EMA impact (causing lower refusal scores across more domains) compared to cybersecurity.
Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets from affected domains can largely restore alignment in those domains, though not always fully.
Concept entanglement at the representation level (using concept vectors) shows that concepts with higher similarity in early layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention.
The phenomenon of EMA is consistent across two model families (Mistral and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to two concepts (Cybersecurity and Safety) and two instruction-tuned aligned models (Qwen-7B-2.5 and Mistral-7B) due to computational resources.
